TRACE targets a reliability gap in multi-step tool-using agents, where unsupported claims, contradictions, repetitive loops, and tool-use anomalies can propagate across long execution trajectories. Existing self-correction methods typically rely on post-hoc reflection or a single intervention mechanism, but do not integrate continuous runtime monitoring, failure attribution, and adaptive recovery in one control layer. TRACE wraps a standard ReAct-style agent with four modules: a Trajectory Monitor, a Failure Attribution module, a Recovery Controller, and an Audit Layer for structured trace logging. We evaluate TRACE on a simulated enterprise incident-triage benchmark of 50 tasks with injected hallucination- and loop-inducing conditions across four difficulty levels. TRACE achieves 76.0% task success versus 68.0% for a self-reflection baseline and 62.0% for vanilla ReAct, while reducing hallucination incidence from 19.4% to 9.6% and loop frequency from 12.1% to 4.8%. The framework is intended for reliable, auditable autonomous execution in engineering environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6997675\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Reactive Agents: Uncertainty-Gated Meta-Reasoning for Tool-Augmented Decision-Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM) agents often plan, act, observe tool feedback, and recover only after errors occur. This reactive design is useful for short horizons but can be brittle in multi-step decision-making where early mistakes compound. This paper studies whether pre-execution uncertainty-aware control and persistent reflective memory can be integrated into a more auditable tool-use controller. We present the Meta-Reasoning Insight Framework (MRIF), a multi-agent architecture that augments a planner–executor loop with an Uncertainty Estimation Module (UEM) for risk gating and a Metacognitive Reflection Loop (MRL) that stores cross-episode experience in a Knowledge Graph. We position MRIFas a systems integration of familiar ideas—uncertainty scoring, reflective updating, and structured memory—rather than as a new agent paradigm. The paper includes a comparative design analysis of representative agent patterns grounded in public artifacts and a limited ToolTalk pilot evaluation against transparent matched-budget baselines. In this pilot, MRIF reaches a 61.3% task success rate, 4.9 absolute points above Metagent-P, with higher tool-call argument accuracy (91.2%) and fewer unnecessary interventions (14.5%). Because the current artifact does not yet include exhaustive ToolTalk coverage, full task identifiers, prompts, seeds, these results should be interpreted as preliminary evidence aboutToolTalk-style tool dialogue rather than as a benchmark ranking or proof of broad generalization.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6997675\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7345744\", \"title\": [\"Robust Scientific AI Agents Under Noisy, Data-Scarce Conditions: Adaptive Model Selection, Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning, and Noise-Robust Surrogate Learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Scientific AI systems are increasingly expected to reason over scarce observations, noisy measurements, unstable simulators, and heterogeneous model families. Existing work usually treats these difficulties separately: robust surrogate models address noisy regression, routing systems select among language models, and control-theoretic allocation methods adapt traffic under non-stationary workloads. This paper argues that noisy, data-scarce scientific workflows require an integrated agent architecture rather than a single fixed predictor. We introduce Robust Scientific AI Agents (RSA-Agents), a framework that represents scientific problem solving as a closed-loop decision process over candidate surrogate models, symbolic tools, validation signals, uncertainty estimates, and execution constraints. The agent maintains a portfolio of candidate scientific models, estimates their task-conditioned reliability from limited evidence, and allocates future calls through a validation-weighted selection rule with persistent exploration. Noise-robust models such as ER-KAN provide the agent with a safer surrogate option when clean-data accuracy is misleading, while adaptive routing and feedback-control principles prevent static model commitments under regime change. In a synthetic pilot benchmark spanning eight analytic functions, three data budgets, and three noise levels, a validation-weighted RSA-Agent reduces mean squared error by 7.7% relative to the best static surrogate overall and by 27.7% in the high-noise setting, while underperforming on clean regimes. These results support the central thesis: robust scientific AI should be evaluated as an adaptive agentic system under uncertainty, not only as a collection of isolated predictors.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7345744\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/cbo9780511794797.007\", \"title\": [\"Reasoning Under Uncertainty\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511794797.007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2010, 4, 19]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "ae59f350101acfe1b0ec0f152e59925da77c7c00a466f2e61ec721928a28f7eb", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6759126", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6997675", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7345744", "doi:10.1017/cbo9780511794797.007"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6997675", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7345744", "https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511794797.007"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
